title: Wrenfield Hotels: why is profit per room down?
prompt: Wrenfield Hotels owns and runs 10 boutique hotels in US cities. This year its hotels were about as busy as last year, yet profit per room fell sharply. The CEO wants to know why, and what to do about it. How would you approach this?

facts.answer: Wrenfield owns and runs 10 boutique hotels in US cities, each with 100 rooms, so 1,000 rooms in total. All hotels are open every night of the year. No hotels opened or closed in either year.
The restaurants and bars are run by a partner that pays Wrenfield a fixed rent. Ignore them; this case is about rooms only.
In both years, 80% of rooms were filled on an average night, at an average price of $250 a night. Guests pay about the same price whichever way they book.
The CEO wants profit per room per night back to last year's $50 within 18 months.
Guests book either directly, through Wrenfield's own website or phone line, or through online travel agencies (booking websites that list many hotels). The booking data by channel is available.
Online travel agencies charge Wrenfield 20% of the room price on every booking they bring. The rate has not changed for several years. Direct bookings have no commission.

In January Wrenfield moved to a new website and booking system. Since then, guests have complained that booking on a phone is slow and often fails; booking on a computer works as before. The number of people visiting the website is about the same as last year.
Wrenfield's web agency says the phone booking problems can be fixed within about three months, for around $300,000.
Hourly wages rose about 5% this year in line with local labour markets. Staffing levels per hotel are unchanged.
New boutique hotels opened in two of Wrenfield's cities, but Wrenfield's occupancy and prices held up. It is not the main issue.

About 40% of guests have stayed with Wrenfield before. Many of them used to book directly, but this year a lot of them booked through travel agencies instead. The agencies mostly bring first-time guests who might not otherwise find Wrenfield.

key_buckets: Revenue: rooms filled (occupancy) and average price
Costs: booking commissions, staff, supplies, building and other costs
Comparison: per room per night, this year versus last year, line by line
What changed: booking channels, the new website, wages
Ways to recover profit: win back direct bookings, cut commissions, control staff costs
good_signs: Starts from profit = revenue minus costs and checks revenue first
Rules out revenue quickly because occupancy and price are flat
Asks to compare costs line by line, year on year
Links the jump in commissions to the shift in how guests book and to the new website
Checks the commission line against the booking mix (80% x $250 x 70% x 20% = $28) rather than taking it on trust
Asks whether website visits changed, to tell fewer visitors apart from fewer bookings per visitor
red_flags: Spends a long time on competitors or prices after hearing they did not change
Treats commissions as fixed costs instead of asking why they rose
Assumes fewer direct bookings means fewer guests, although occupancy is unchanged
Jumps to cutting staff without diagnosing the cause

exhibits.title: Profit per room per night, averaged over all rooms ($)
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask for revenue and costs per room, this year versus last year, or for a breakdown of costs.
exhibits.insight: Revenue is flat at $200 per room per night (80% of rooms filled at $250), but profit fell $20, from $50 to $30, and the margin from 25% to 15%. Booking commissions rose $16 and staff $4 (the 5% wage rise); all other costs are unchanged.

exhibits.title: How guests booked: share of room nights by channel
exhibits.reveal_hint: Ask why booking commissions rose, or how guests booked this year versus last year.
exhibits.insight: Direct bookings fell from 70% to 30% of nights, and online travel agencies rose from 30% to 70%, at an unchanged 20% commission. That explains the whole commission rise: $200 x 70% x 20% = $28 per room per night, against $200 x 30% x 20% = $12 last year. With website visits flat and phone booking failing since the January relaunch, the new website is the likely cause.

math.question: By what percentage did profit per room per night fall?
math.working: Profit fell from $50 to $30, a fall of $20. $20 / $50 = 40%.

math.question: What percentage of the fall in profit is explained by higher booking commissions?
math.working: Commissions rose $16 ($28 - $12). Profit fell $20. $16 / $20 = 80%. The other $4 is the rise in staff costs.

math.question: Across all 1,000 rooms, how much less profit is Wrenfield making in a year, in $ million?
math.working: $20 less per room per night x 1,000 rooms = $20,000 a night. x 365 nights = $7.3 million a year.

math.question: If Wrenfield won back enough direct bookings that only half of all nights came through travel agencies, with everything else as it is this year, what would profit per room per night be, in dollars?
math.working: Commission would be $200 x 50% x 20% = $20 per room per night, down from $28. Profit rises by $8, from $30 to $38. Getting all the way back to 70% direct would give $46; the last $4 needs work on staff costs.

brainstorm.question: How could Wrenfield win back direct bookings and cut what it pays in commission?
idea_bank: Fix the new website's phone booking as the top priority, and test it on real phones
Put the old booking system back on phones until the new one works
Offer perks only for direct bookings, such as free breakfast, late check-out or a room upgrade
Promise the best price on Wrenfield's own website, or a members-only rate, once the agency contracts have been checked
Start a simple loyalty programme for repeat guests that rewards booking direct
Email past guests with an offer to book direct
Invite guests who came through travel agencies to book direct next time, for example at check-out
Run search ads on Wrenfield's own name so people reach its website, not an agency
Negotiate a lower commission with the travel agencies, or offer them fewer rooms at busy times
Keep the agencies for first-time guests, and focus on moving repeat guests back to direct
Make the phone booking line easy to reach and well staffed
Recover the staff cost rise through rotas matched to occupancy, or a small rate rise, since wages rose across the market

must_mention: Profit per room per night fell $20 (from $50 to $30, down 40%) while revenue stayed flat
Higher commissions explain $16 of the fall (80%), because bookings shifted from direct to online travel agencies after the new website made booking on phones hard
A clear recommendation: fix the website and win back direct bookings first, with next steps
good_signs: Sizes the problem: about $7.3 million a year across the group, against a website fix of about $300,000
Shows the payoff: back to half direct gives $38 a night; back to 70% direct gives $46
Keeps the travel agencies for first-time guests and aims to win repeat guests back to direct, rather than dropping the agencies
Deals with the $4 rise in staff costs separately and names what to track, such as the weekly share of direct bookings and phone booking success

model_answer_outline: Clarify the goal (profit per room per night back to $50 within 18 months) and confirm that occupancy, prices and the number of hotels are unchanged.
Structure: profit = revenue minus costs. Revenue (80% occupancy x $250 = $200 per room per night) is flat, so focus on costs line by line.
Analysis: profit fell $20 (40%). Booking commissions rose $16 and staff $4; everything else is flat. Commissions explain 80% of the fall.

Root cause: direct bookings fell from 70% to 30% of nights after the new website made booking on phones hard, while website visits held steady and many repeat guests switched to agencies. Agencies charge an unchanged 20%, so commission rose from $200 x 30% x 20% = $12 to $200 x 70% x 20% = $28 per room per night.

Size and payoff: $20 x 1,000 rooms x 365 nights = $7.3 million a year, so the $300,000 website fix pays for itself within weeks once bookings return. Getting back to half direct lifts profit to $38; back to 70% direct gives $46.

Recommendation (answer first): this is a booking-channel problem caused by the new website, not a demand problem. Fix phone booking within three months (or put the old system back meanwhile), then win repeat guests back with perks for booking direct, emails to past guests and a loyalty programme, while keeping the agencies for first-time guests. Recover the last $4 through rotas matched to occupancy or a small rate rise, since the wage rise is market-wide.

Risks and next steps: guests used to booking through agencies may be slow to come back, and agency contracts may limit lower direct prices, so check them first. Track the weekly share of direct bookings and phone booking success against the 70% target, with $50 a night due within 18 months.
